newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe to boost investment drive, eyes East, U.S.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe to boost investment drive, eyes East, U.S.

text.p: Zimbabwe's chief investment scouting officer said on Wednesday the southern African state was drawing up a fresh plan to boost its drive for new business, with a special eye on the Far East and the United States.

Nicholas Ncube, director of the Zimbabwe Investment Centre (ZIC), told Reuters that potential foreign investors, especially in Western Europe and South East Asia, had shown great interest and confidence in Zimbabwe in the last four years.
"We are putting the gloss on an 18-month plan which will see us consolidating in the areas where we have been very active, and also see us expanding into new areas," he said in an interview.
"Specifically, we need to work hard in the Far East and also in the United States," he added.
Ncube's state-funded centre was set up in 1994 to try and lure vital foreign investment into an economy that had been devastated by 15 years of world sanctions against previous white minority rule.
This was followed by President Robert Mugabe's government's disastrous 10-year experiment with socialism that was abandoned in 1990, intermittent droughts and alleged state mismanagement.

Zimbabwe introduced free market reforms in 1991 with the backing of key Western donors, including the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which Ncube said laid the foundation for the country's current investment drive.
The five-year economic reform programme got rid of stiff pricing controls, foreign exchange rationing, import licensing and liberalised rules on profit and dividend remittance among others.

"We had hit rock bottom...and now we are starting to see some positive growth in the economy. With more reforms we are heading for sustainable growth," Ncube said of plans by the government to launch another reform scheme this year.

The new reforms have been delayed by the government's failure to win donor funding which has been made conditional on big cuts in state expenditure, accounting for about 38 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

Zimbabwe's agriculture-powered economy has grown at less than two percent annually over the last 10 years, but last year it posted an eight percent rise in GDP and growth is seen at around five percent in 1997 following another good rainy season.

"The government is working on the fundamentals -- inflation, the budget deficit (seen rising to 12 percent from 10.1 percent last year against a target of 8.5 percent), interest rates and a battle against these will get us more investment," Ncube said.

He said Western Europe and South East Asia, where the government has held investment promotion conferences in Britain, Germany, Austria and Malaysia in the last three years, were showing interest and confidence in the Zimbabwean economy.

There was great interest in investing in tourism, mining, construction, agro-industry, information technology and energy, he said, adding that many potential investors were keen on joint ventures with Zimbabwean partners.
Ncube said a five-year tax holiday for both domestic and foreign investors in infrastructural development had seen many local farmers building much-needed dams.

There would be greater investment opportunities once Zimbabwe's long-awaited privatisation scheme gathered pace, he said. Investor confidence was illustrated by a 10 times oversubscription for shares in dairy company Dairibord, the first state enterprise to be privatised.

Official statistics show that ZIC has approved new investment worth Z$5.4 billion (U.S.$474.5 million) out of 223 projects in the first six months of 1997 compared to Z$6.3 billion ($557.5 million) out of 261 projects in the same period last year.
